title: "Our Analysis"
subtitle: "Methods and Evaluation"

## Creating Target Destination Groups

We needed a sensible way to group hundreds of different colleges and universities into a handful of meaningful categories. With stakeholder input, we landed on four main destination categories:

- **NW5**:  Willamette's closest private peer institutions in the Pacific
  Northwest (Reed College, Lewis & Clark College, Whitman College, and
  University of Puget Sound)
- **Three Large Public**: Oregon State University, University of Oregon,
  and Portland State University
- **Local Public**: other public colleges in Oregon and Washington
- **Local Private**: other private colleges in Oregon and Washington

We analyzed two destination groupings as part of an iterative refinement process. Our first version cast a wider geographic net and included students' campus-visit history as a predictive feature. After reviewing early results with our stakeholder at Willamette, we narrowed the geography to just Oregon and Washington and limited our features to information that's available *at the time a student applies*. Both versions told a consistent story; the second, refined version is what's presented on the Findings page.

## Looking for Natural Groupings in the Data

We used a clustering technique to see whether applicants naturally sort
themselves into distinct groups based on their profile alone (without
knowing where they enrolled). This produced four fairly evenly sized groups, with Figure 1 showing five features found strongly influential in differentiating clusters: academic strength, financial need, and application creation timeline.

![Figure 1: Cluster Profiles (Standardized)](/images/cluster_profile_heatmap.png)

The heatmap shows how each cluster compares to the overall applicant population, with red indicating a higher-than-average value and blue indicating a lower-than-average value.

We then checked whether those clusters lined up with actual enrollment
destinations, and validated the results using a standard statistical test (chi-square, with a measure called Cramer's V for how *strong* the relationship is).

![Figure 2: Cluster Membership by Destination Category](/images/cluster_destination_mix_grouped.png)

The relationship was statistically real (p-value of < 0.05) but practically weak (Cramer's V of 0.076), meaning cluster membership alone is not a strong standalone predictor of enrollment destination. This told us we needed a more targeted predictive model rather than relying on broad applicant groupings.

## Building a Predictive Model

We compared three modeling approaches to see which best predicted an
applicant's likely destination:

- **Multinomial Logistic Regression**: serves as an interpretable baseline for the multi-class outcome that predicts an enrollment destination group.
- **Support Vector Machine (SVM)**:  an alternative classifier 
- **XGBoost**: a more sophisticated model well-suited to handling missing
  data, which is common in application records

Models were evaluated using an 80/20 train-test split to ensure that there is adequate data to validate against, with no separate validation set held out. 

For each model, we measured overall accuracy and looked closely at how well
it performed *per destination category*, since we didn't want a model that
only did well on the most common outcome. See [Findings](findings.qmd) for more information on what we found about applicant behavior.

For the full technical detail on both destination category versions, see our
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/Data-Science-Capstone-Project-2026/Public_Repository/tree/main/src).
